label: The verdict table across iterations 1-4 is 41 findings: 0 covered, 6 partial, 3 contradictions and 32 lacks (iteration 1: 9 findings, 0/3/1/5; iteration 2: 12, 0/1/0/11; iteration 3: 10, 0/1/2/7; iteration 4: 10, 0/1/0/9); the shape of the result is the finding, because the sk-code Rust set is not wrong about ports, it is silent about them.

The sk-code Rust set has no CLI argument design at all (zero hits for clap), while rust-anything supplies both halves: its own CLI is derive-first with #[derive(Parser)], #[command(name, version, about, after_help)], a Subcommand enum whose variant doc comments are the help text and ValueEnum for closed sets, and app front-door scaffolds a clap parser for the commands and flags in the recorded cases.

The sk-code Rust set has no terminal rendering and rust-anything does not supply it either: zero hits for ratatui and crossterm, the only terminal matches are 'terminal key' in sort-comparator prose, and rust-anything's own output is plain writeln! through a say! macro that stops quietly when stdout is closed; this is the one app-style gap rust-anything cannot fill, so the edit must be sourced from the ratatui and crossterm documentation.

The sk-code Rust set has no exit-code contract for a binary: its only mention sits inside a sidecar-protocol rule ('Sidecar protocols must define framing, encoding, field order, newline behavior, exit codes, and stderr behavior'), while rust-anything treats the exit code as part of the recorded contract because the front door passes it through and app replay exits non-zero on any mismatch.

The sk-code Rust set has no signal handling and rust-anything does not supply it either: zero hits for signal, SIGINT or Ctrl-C, and rust-anything's nearest rule is about child processes ('Run every outside program through crate::process, which closes stdin and stops it at a time limit') rather than signals, so the edit must be sourced elsewhere.

The sk-code Rust set has no stdout/stderr split rule, while rust-anything carries a hard-won one: a test command's output corrupted the MCP stream because the child wrote to the server's stdout, so every child's stdout must go to stderr or a pipe and never to the protocol stream; the rule generalises to any program that owns a protocol stream.
The sk-code Rust set has no is_terminal or NO_COLOR rule and rust-anything does not supply it either (zero hits for both).
The sk-code Rust set has no progress-reporting rule and rust-anything does not supply it either (zero hits for progress).

The sk-code Rust set has no size budget for a port, which matters more for an app than for a binding; rust-anything's gate fails a port at most 3x the original's lines plus 50 for imports and signatures, with the remedy to use the crates analyze lists and fold repeated code.

The sk-code Rust set has no CLI golden-case format and rust-anything's is directly reusable: app cases are trycmd files in rust/app-cases/ with <case>.toml (argv, env, exit code), .stdin, .stdout, .stderr, .in/ and .out/, editable by hand and runnable from a Rust test with trycmd once the port has a binary.

The sk-code Rust set has no rule that a replay report is a committed CI artifact; rust-anything commits replay-report.md and runs git diff --exit-code on it in CI so a half-ported app fails CI on any change in what passes, better or worse, until the report is updated, which is the app-scale version of the cheat guard.

The sk-code Rust set has no fallback-rate metric, which is the only progress signal a half-ported app has; rust-anything's front door counts each fallback to the original and reports the rate, and app replay reports it for any build that appends to RUST_ANYTHING_FALLBACK_LOG.
